title: GlusterFS on Kubernetes: Why Node-Local Bricks and Stable Identity Matter
summary: A practical look at running a three-node GlusterFS cluster on Kubernetes, including node-local persistent bricks, StatefulSet identity, readiness, networking, and operational limits.
author: Eliware
content:
# GlusterFS on Kubernetes: Why Node-Local Bricks and Stable Identity Matter

Running GlusterFS on Kubernetes is not the same as running a stateless web service. A GlusterFS node has storage identity, peer relationships, brick data, volume definitions, network addresses, and recovery behavior that must survive more than one container restart.

The central design question is simple:

> Which physical or node-local storage owns each brick, and how will Kubernetes preserve that relationship?

The Eliware project uses a deliberately small model: three GlusterFS server instances, one per worker, each backed by its own node-local persistent volume. The design is aimed at teams operating their own Kubernetes infrastructure and wanting shared filesystem semantics from storage they control.

It is experimental and deployment-specific. The goal of this article is not to claim that GlusterFS is the right storage layer for every Kubernetes cluster. It is to explain the decisions that make this particular architecture understandable and testable.

## The basic topology

The cluster has three GlusterFS nodes and one brick on each node:

```text
Kubernetes worker 1       Kubernetes worker 2       Kubernetes worker 3
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│ GlusterFS node 1 │      │ GlusterFS node 2 │      │ GlusterFS node 3 │
│ /var/lib/glusterd│      │ /var/lib/glusterd│      │ /var/lib/glusterd│
│ /data/brick1     │      │ /data/brick1     │      │ /data/brick1     │
│ node-local PV    │      │ node-local PV    │      │ node-local PV    │
└────────┬─────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘
         └────────────── replica-3 volume ────────────────┘
```

The important part is not the diagram’s symmetry. It is the ownership boundary. Each brick remains on the node-local persistent storage intended for that GlusterFS node. Application pods do not browse or write the brick directory directly. They use a GlusterFS client mount or an explicitly configured access layer such as NFS-Ganesha.

## Why node-local storage matters

A brick is not just an arbitrary directory that happens to be visible from a pod. It is part of the GlusterFS volume definition and is managed by the GlusterFS server that owns it. If the storage underneath that brick moves unexpectedly, disappears, or is presented to a different node with a different identity, the cluster can lose the assumptions it used to coordinate the volume.

Node-local persistent volumes make the placement relationship explicit:

- worker 1 owns node 1’s brick storage;
- worker 2 owns node 2’s brick storage; and
- worker 3 owns node 3’s brick storage.

This does not make the storage automatically safe. It makes the failure domain visible. You still need to understand what happens when a worker, disk, Kubernetes control plane, network, or storage provisioner fails.

Do not place a brick on an application pod’s ephemeral filesystem. Do not point a brick at a shared path that is simultaneously mounted and modified outside GlusterFS. Do not assume that three directories on one worker provide the same protection as three bricks across three workers.

## Persist both data and identity

A GlusterFS node has more than its user data. Its `/var/lib/glusterd` state includes the control-plane information that describes peers, volumes, and brick relationships. The brick filesystem contains the actual volume data and GlusterFS metadata.

The Eliware image persists both:

- node-local brick data; and
- the node’s GlusterFS control-plane database.

That distinction matters after container recreation. Recreating a pod should not silently erase the peer identity and volume definitions that tell the cluster what the brick is. A new container process is not necessarily a new storage node.

In Kubernetes terms, stable StatefulSet identity and correctly bound persistent volumes are part of the storage design, not incidental deployment details. A pod ordinal, PVC binding, hostname, and GlusterFS peer identity need to remain aligned.

## StatefulSet is useful, but not sufficient

A StatefulSet can provide stable pod names, ordered identity, and predictable PVC relationships. Those properties are helpful for a clustered storage service. They do not, by themselves, solve:

- brick network reachability;
- advertised GlusterFS addresses;
- storage placement;
- host security labels;
- peer formation;
- volume healing;
- node replacement; or
- backup and restore.

A StatefulSet gives you a framework for identity. You must still design the storage and network contracts around it.

When a node is replaced, ask what should happen to its identity and data. A fresh pod with an empty PVC is not an equivalent replacement for a pod whose original brick data and `/var/lib/glusterd` state remain intact. If the operational answer is “restore the node from backup,” document and test that procedure.

## Discovery and brick traffic in Kubernetes

GlusterFS clients first discover the volume and then connect to the brick processes. A Kubernetes Service that exposes only the discovery path is not automatically enough for native clients.

The client must be able to reach:

- the discovery endpoint;
- each advertised GlusterFS node address; and
- the configured brick-port range on those addresses.

The Eliware storage contract uses TCP `24007` for discovery and TCP `49152–49157` for the current brick range. The discovery endpoint is not a proxy for direct brick traffic. Kubernetes network policy, pod routing, host firewalls, and security groups must permit the full client-to-brick path.

This is one reason to publish stable per-node native endpoints rather than relying on a single virtual address to represent every storage connection. The addresses returned in the GlusterFS volume configuration must be useful from the client network.

For a deeper explanation, read [GlusterFS Networking Explained: Why Port 24007 Alone Is Not Enough](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/).

## Readiness is a storage contract

A container process can be alive while the storage service is not ready. Kubernetes probes should reflect that difference.

The Eliware image exposes separate concepts:

- `/healthz` is a liveness check;
- `/readyz` is a readiness check; and
- `/health` serves the operator dashboard.

Readiness can require:

- a live GlusterFS daemon;
- connected peers;
- a started volume;
- online bricks; and
- an available shared-state mount when shared state is required.

This prevents a console or dependent service from receiving traffic merely because Node.js is still running. It also avoids using liveness as a blunt mechanism for every dependency failure. A temporary peer or mount problem should be visible as degraded readiness rather than automatically turning every problem into a process restart.

At the same time, repeated unexpected GlusterFS failure should have a bounded recovery path. The local supervisor retries configured recovery and can exit after its retry budget is exhausted so Kubernetes can replace the pod. An intentional administrative stop is kept distinct from an unexpected crash.

That distinction is small in configuration and large in operations:

```text
Intentional down  ──> keep the console available for administration
Unexpected exit   ──> retry, then allow Kubernetes replacement
Unavailable state ──> fail readiness, not necessarily liveness
```

## Keep shared state separate from application data

The default replica-3 `gluster` volume is reserved for shared console state. It stores users, sessions, audit data, metadata, locks, and related control-plane files.

Application workloads receive separate volumes. A media workload should not share the protected control-plane volume merely because both need a filesystem. Separate volumes give operators clearer boundaries for:

- permissions;
- quotas;
- lifecycle;
- performance tuning;
- backup policy; and
- destructive operations.

The shared state volume is intentionally low-throughput control-plane storage. It is not a general-purpose database volume, and the architecture should not be read as a recommendation to run SQLite or another database over GlusterFS without workload-specific testing.

## Brick paths belong to the storage layer

The operator console derives application brick paths below the configured node-local brick root from the configured Gluster peers. Ordinary operators enter a display name, not a list of server-side brick paths.

This reduces the chance that a routine volume request will accidentally:

- place a brick outside the intended persistent volume;
- reuse a path belonging to another volume;
- put multiple replicas on one failure domain; or
- expose a host path that the storage policy does not permit.

Trusted administrative automation can still perform explicit brick operations, but those actions remain validated and scoped. A convenience form should not weaken the storage contract.

## SELinux and host security are part of the design

On SELinux-enforcing hosts, brick roots need the correct persistent label for GlusterFS. A path that exists and is mounted is not necessarily usable by the GlusterFS daemon under the host security policy.

The project keeps new console-created bricks below the configured brick root and applies the expected storage labeling workflow. Deployment teams should still verify the actual policy, mount options, security context, and host configuration for their distribution and Kubernetes runtime.

Do not treat privileged containers as a substitute for understanding host security. Privilege may make a local test work while masking a production policy or isolation problem.

## NFS-Ganesha is a separate access layer

Some Kubernetes or external clients need NFS rather than a native GlusterFS mount. The project can use NFS-Ganesha with the Gluster FSAL as an optional layer.

That choice introduces another service and another network path:

```text
Native client  ───────────────> GlusterFS bricks
NFS client     ── TCP 2049 ──> NFS-Ganesha ──> GlusterFS
```

NFS-Ganesha does not make brick placement irrelevant, and it does not automatically provide shared failover state for client sessions. Validate export configuration, access controls, service availability, and workload behavior separately. The Compose topology leaves NFS disabled by default.

## Where this architecture fits

This design is a reasonable evaluation target when you:

- operate your own Kubernetes nodes;
- have dedicated node-local storage;
- need shared filesystem semantics;
- can permit direct client-to-brick traffic;
- are willing to test failure and recovery; and
- want an inspectable storage layer rather than a black box.

It may be a poor fit when you:

- need object-storage semantics rather than a filesystem;
- cannot operate privileged or stateful storage workloads;
- require a managed service with vendor-operated recovery;
- need database-specific consistency and latency guarantees; or
- cannot provide independent backups and maintenance procedures.

GlusterFS is a storage building block, not a universal answer to Kubernetes persistence. Selecting it should follow the workload and operational model, not precede them.

## What to test before production

A serious evaluation should include more than a successful pod start:

- recreate a GlusterFS container while preserving its PVC;
- reboot or drain one worker;
- verify that each brick returns with the expected identity;
- test a node or disk failure;
- observe replica healing;
- test client behavior during degraded service;
- verify readiness and liveness transitions;
- test the full discovery and brick network path;
- exercise access permissions and audit records;
- validate NFS-Ganesha only if you plan to use it; and
- restore an independent backup.

Use disposable data first. Record the results and the time required for recovery. A storage design is not validated by architecture diagrams alone.

## The design in one sentence

The Eliware approach is intentionally straightforward: keep each GlusterFS identity and brick on its intended node-local persistent volume, keep control-plane state separate from application data, expose the full network path, and let Kubernetes manage processes without pretending it manages storage decisions for you.

If you are new to the project, start with [GlusterFS on EL10: Install It and Create Your First Replica-3 Volume](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/) and the official [GlusterFS architecture guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Quick-Start-Guide/Architecture/).
